You are going to turn a recipe into a Rhylthyme program: parallel **tracks** of sequential **steps**, each with a duration and a start trigger, that one person follows against a live clock.

Plan this as a Rhylthyme recipe and deliver a live timeline: Three-Course Dinner for Six: Two Burners, One Oven for 6 people, three courses
Resource limits: one oven, two burners, one cook, courses go out in order.
Everything must be finished by 19:30.

Source text (read all of it):
<<<
Three-Course Dinner for Six: Two Burners, One Oven

Guests sit down at half past seven. There are two burners, one oven and one cook, so the oven does the braise first and the tart second, and the burners are rarely both free.

Mise en place
Chop the mirepoix, trim the short ribs and measure the stock: forty minutes of knife work before anything goes on the heat.

Main: braised short ribs
Heat the oven to 300°F; give it 20 minutes. Sear the short ribs in a heavy pot over high heat for 12 minutes, turning once. Lift the ribs out, soften the mirepoix in the same pot for 8 minutes, add the wine and reduce it for 5 minutes, then return the ribs with the stock. Braise the ribs, covered, for 3 hours. Rest the pot off the heat for 20 minutes, then skim the fat and reduce the braising liquid for 15 minutes.

Starter: leek and potato soup
Two hours into the braise, sweat the sliced leeks in butter for 10 minutes. Add the potatoes and the stock and simmer for 30 minutes, then blend the soup smooth; 5 minutes. Hold it warm on the back burner until the guests are seated.

Dessert: apple tart
Roll the pastry and line the tin; 15 minutes. Chill the shell in the refrigerator for at least 30 minutes and no more than two hours. Slice the apples and arrange them in the shell; 20 minutes. Bake the tart for 45 minutes the moment the ribs leave the oven, while the ribs are resting.

Service
Ladle the soup when everyone is seated; ten minutes at the table. Plate the ribs ten minutes after the soup bowls are cleared, and give the plating five minutes. Let the main course run as long as it runs. The tart goes out twenty minutes after the main plates come back; ten minutes to slice and serve.
>>>

Read all of it before you answer. Then say back, in one paragraph and in your own words: what is being made, for how many (or at what scale), by when, and under what constraints — equipment that exists only once, how many people are working, anything that has to be held, rested or ready at a particular moment. If the text you were given looks truncated, or points at a section that is not here, say so instead of filling the gap.

```json

}
```

The source text is a complete recipe plan for a three-course dinner for six guests—leek and potato soup, braised short ribs, and apple tart—that must be ready and served in course order by 19:30, with guests seated at 19:30. It assumes a single cook and only one oven and two burners, so the oven is reserved first for the 3-hour braise and then for the 45-minute tart bake, while the burners are constantly contested. Several dishes must be timed to a held or ready state: the soup is started mid-braise and held warm until seating; the braised ribs are rested 20 minutes, then skimmed and reduced; the tart shell must chill for at least 30 minutes and no more than 2 hours before baking, and the tart must begin baking exactly when the ribs leave the oven. Service also follows a sequence: soup at seating, ribs 10 minutes after soup bowls are cleared, main course duration unspecified, and tart 20 minutes after main plates are returned.

```json
{
  "summary": "A three-course dinner for six people is being made: leek and potato soup, braised short ribs, and apple tart. Everything must be finished by 19:30, when guests are seated, and courses must go out in order. The kitchen has one oven, two burners, and one cook, so oven time must be sequenced and the burners are a shared bottleneck. The soup must be held warm until guests are seated; the ribs must rest for 20 minutes, then be skimmed and reduced; the tart must chill for at least 30 minutes and no more than 2 hours, then bake for 45 minutes as soon as the ribs leave the oven.",
  "servesOrScale": "6 people",
  "deadline": "19:30",
  "constraints": [
    "one oven",
    "two burners",
    "one cook",
    "courses must be served in order",
    "soup must be held warm until guests are seated",
    "braised ribs must rest for 20 minutes after the braise",
    "rib braising liquid must be skimmed and reduced for 15 minutes",
    "tart shell must chill for at least 30 minutes and no more than 2 hours",
    "tart must begin baking when the ribs leave the oven",
    "service timing depends on table clearance between courses"
  ]
}
```

A track is a single sequential lane of work; steps inside the same track cannot overlap, and any work that happens while something else is happening must live in a separate track. A step has exactly one duration kind: `fixed` with a `seconds` value, `variable` with `minSeconds`, `maxSeconds`, and `defaultSeconds`, or `indefinite`, which runs until the person ends it. A `startTrigger` connects a step to the clock or to another step, using types such as `programStart`, `programStartOffset`, `afterStep`, `afterStepWithBuffer`, `manual`, `onAbort`, or `compound`. `stepId` values are unique across the whole program, not just within a track, and `afterStep` references must point to existing steps without creating cycles. Every `task` used by a step must have a matching `resourceConstraints` entry, and that entry’s `maxConcurrent` controls how many steps can occupy that same resource at once. Repeated work should be represented by one step with `replicates`, using `instances: "each"` for follow-on per-instance work, `instances: "all"` for a barrier, and `maxInFlight` when a holding area or staging space can only accommodate a limited number of items at a time.

Expected resource constraints for this dinner:

- `oven` — `maxConcurrent: 1` — there is only one oven, so the braise and the tart bake compete for it.
- `burner` — `maxConcurrent: 2` — there are two burners total; searing, sweating, simmering, reducing, and holding soup can share them, but never more than two at once.
- `cook` — `maxConcurrent: 1` — there is one cook, so all hands-on active work should be treated as a single-person bottleneck unless a step is passive.
- `fridge` — `maxConcurrent: 1` — the tart shell needs refrigerated chilling, which can be modeled as a passive occupying step.
- `actors` — `1` — only one person is working.

```json
{
  "acknowledgement": "tracks are sequential lines of work; one duration kind per step; triggers link steps; every task needs a resourceConstraint; stepIds are global",
  "resourceConstraints": [
    { "task": "oven", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "burner", "maxConcurrent": 2 },
    { "task": "cook", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "fridge", "maxConcurrent": 1 }
  ],
  "actors": 1
}
```
